clue.text: "If any be 's legs, these are they. Thou art very — indeed!" (The Tempest)

definitions.text: "If any be 's legs, these are they. Thou art very — indeed!" (The Tempest)

parts.words: "If any be 's legs, these are they. Thou art very — indeed!" (The Tempest)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Stephano, finding the jester under Caliban's cloak, names him twice in these lines

explanation.surface: A line from The Tempest with the speaker's friend's name left out twice.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver supplies the missing name from Act 2 of The Tempest, where the drunken butler recognises his companion, the king's jester.
explanation.definitionFit: The gaps in Stephano's speech are filled by the name of Alonso's jester in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Bengali polymath in Ortega rewrite

indicators.note: to rewrite a name is to set its letters down again in a new order

explanation.surface: An Indian sage appears in a revised edition of the Spanish philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabindranath Tagore was the Bengali poet, painter and composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabindranath was a Bengali poet, musician and artist, and a Nobel laureate in literature.

clue.text: Jessica Lange and Halle Berry were involved in losing him

definitions.text: Jessica Lange and Halle Berry were involved in losing him

parts.words: Jessica Lange and Halle Berry were involved in losing him
parts.note: the two actresses starred in a 1995 film about a custody battle whose title names the boy at its centre after a prophet

explanation.surface: Two actresses were to blame for a man going missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The film is Losing Isaiah, from Seth Margolis's novel; the clue's 'involved' means 'starred'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adopted boy in the film shares his name with the Old Testament prophet.

clue.text: Solicit some verse from Lady Montagu

definitions.text: Solicit some verse from Lady Montagu

parts.note: to court is to woo or seek favour
a poem is a piece of verse

explanation.surface: Ask the letter-writer Lady Mary for a few lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's satirical Court Poems were published by Curll in 1716.
explanation.definitionFit: Montagu's satires on royal society were printed as Court Poems, so each is a royal-circle verse.

clue.text: Tip never refused by her

parts.note: in Dickens's novel the heroine's feckless brother Edward is nicknamed Tip, and she indulges him endlessly

explanation.surface: She always accepted gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like a gratuity, but it is the nickname of Amy Dorrit's idle brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Amy, the devoted daughter of the Marshalsea in Dickens, always helped her brother.

clue.text: He was translated for a queen

definitions.text: He was translated for a queen

parts.words: He was translated for a queen
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the weaver is given an ass's head, Quince crying 'thou art translated', and the fairy queen Titania dotes on him

explanation.surface: Someone's work was rendered into another language for a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' suggests languages, but Shakespeare uses it to mean transformed: Puck turns the weaver into an ass for Titania, queen of the fairies, to fall in love with.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick, the weaver of Athens, is the character transformed and loved by the fairy queen.

clue.text: Kipling's ballad captain offers a single article from Italy

parts.note: one is a single unit
il is the Italian definite article

explanation.surface: A Kipling seaman gives one Italian piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain O'Neil appears in Kipling's verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish sea captain named in Kipling's ballad verse bears this surname.

clue.text: Stevenson in Samoa?

parts.note: the Samoans called Robert Louis Stevenson Tusitala, teller of tales

explanation.surface: A question about the novelist's last years in the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual sense, a sneak, is beside the point: read as two words it renders Tusitala, his Samoan name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's Samoan name means story-teller, which split in two gives a sneak's word.

clue.text: "- is only the string that ties the robber's bundle" (Shelley)

definitions.text: "- is only the string that ties the robber's bundle" (Shelley)

parts.words: "- is only the string that ties the robber's bundle" (Shelley)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Shelley's notes to Queen Mab attacking rule by a king

explanation.surface: Shelley's radical line on what holds a thief's loot together.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley attacks rule by a crowned sovereign as merely binding together the spoils of robbery.

clue.text: Webb's character has progressed, to some degree

definitions.meaning: Charles Webb's 1963 novel, later the Mike Nichols film, is named after its hero Benjamin Braddock's status
one who has moved on to a university degree, with 'to some degree' feigning to mean 'somewhat'

explanation.surface: A novelist's hero has developed somewhat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to some degree' reads as 'partly' but literally means arriving at an academic degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin is the title figure of Webb's novel, and anyone who has completed a degree course holds that title.

clue.text: It was a game to Deighton

definitions.text: It was a game to Deighton

parts.words: It was a game to Deighton
parts.note: Len Deighton's spy novel of 1983 is titled after the divided German capital followed by the word Game

explanation.surface: A thriller writer treated something as mere sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Len Deighton wrote the Bernard Samson trilogy beginning with this city's Game, followed by Mexico Set and London Match.
explanation.definitionFit: The German capital is the city named in the title of Deighton's novel of Cold War espionage.

clue.text: Hit for Garbo as O'Neill's original Chris Christopherson

definitions.text: Hit for Garbo as O'Neill's original Chris Christopherson

parts.words: Hit for Garbo as O'Neill's original Chris Christopherson
parts.note: Eugene O'Neill rewrote his play Chris Christopherson into a drama named for the sailor's daughter, filmed in 1930 as Garbo's first talkie

explanation.surface: A box-office success for the Swedish star as a playwright's original character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garbo talks!' was the slogan for the 1930 film; O'Neill's earlier version of the play bore the father's name.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Neill's play about a Swedish barge captain's daughter was Garbo's 1930 talking-picture success.

clue.text: Lamb associated with this pork

parts.note: Charles Lamb's essay A Dissertation upon ... Pig tells how the Chinese discovered cooked pork by burning down a house

explanation.surface: Meat from one animal paired with meat from another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb' looks like meat to go with the pork, but it is Charles Lamb, the essayist of Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamb's comic essay celebrates pig cooked in the oven or over a fire.

clue.text: Get together afterwards for creator of Juan

parts.note: to link is to join or connect
later means at a subsequent time

explanation.surface: Meet up later with the man who invented Juan.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Linklater, the Scottish novelist, wrote Juan in America and Juan in China.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish novelist Eric wrote the comic Juan novels about Juan Motley.

clue.text: Slender hints at this rabbit trapper and his colleagues

definitions.text: Slender hints at this rabbit trapper and his colleagues

parts.words: Slender hints at this rabbit trapper and his colleagues
parts.note: in The Merry Wives of Windsor Slender calls Falstaff's men, Bardolph among them, 'coney-catching rascals', a coney being a rabbit and coney-catching meaning cheating

explanation.surface: A thin man drops hints about a poacher and his mates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slender' looks like an adjective but is Abraham Slender of The Merry Wives; 'rabbit trapper' renders the Elizabethan 'coney-catcher', a swindler.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-nosed follower of Falstaff shares his name with the noble rebel of Henry IV, here given his title.

clue.text: Hoped I managed to get transport for a son of Priam

indicators.note: managed means handled or arranged, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a bus is a means of transport

explanation.surface: Someone hoped to catch a lift for one of the Trojan princes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'managed' is the anagram signal on 'Hoped I'. Deiphobus, Hector's brother, married Helen after Paris died and was killed when Troy fell.
explanation.definitionFit: Deiphobus was a Trojan prince, brother of Hector, who wed Helen after the death of Paris.

clue.text: Greer's race

parts.note: Germaine Greer's 1979 book on women painters was titled The ... Race

explanation.surface: A competition run by the feminist writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race' looks complete, but it completes Greer's title The Obstacle Race.
explanation.definitionFit: Greer's book title pairs the hurdle with race, a barrier women painters faced.

clue.text: Princely refugee from Happy Valley

parts.note: in Samuel Johnson's fable an Abyssinian prince escapes the idle comfort of the Happy Valley

explanation.surface: A royal fugitive leaves a contented place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy Valley' sounds like a colonial Kenyan set but is Johnson's Abyssinian paradise.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's Abyssinian prince flees the confines of the Happy Valley in search of happiness.

clue.text: Fine French month is a reversal for dramatist

indicators.note: the two little words are swapped round in order, as the word 'reversal' instructs

parts.note: beau is French for fine or handsome
March is the third month

explanation.surface: A good French month turns out badly for a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is a reversal' reads as 'proves a setback', but 'reversal' swaps the two words 'is a', giving A then IS. Beaumarchais wrote The Barber of Seville and The Marriage of Figaro.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Beaumarchais was the French playwright behind the Figaro comedies.

clue.text: Novel heroine recalls compiler, inter alia

indicators.note: the Latin word for among signals putting one piece between the letters of another

parts.note: the compiler, the setter, refers to self as me

explanation.surface: A heroine of fiction brings to mind the setter, among other things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inter alia' reads as the Latin tag, but 'inter' puts ME into ALIA. Amelia is Fielding's last novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Fielding's last novel takes its title from its long-suffering heroine Amelia Booth.

clue.text: Speaks tediously for part of session

parts.note: pro means in favour of

indicators.note: only a portion of the following word is taken, its opening letters

explanation.surface: Someone drones on through part of a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: To prose is to talk or write in a dull, long-winded way.

clue.text: Opera in two comebacks for conductor

parts.note: Tosca is Puccini's opera

indicators.note: the reversed word is used twice over, as 'two' says
a comeback goes back the way it came, so the little word is read backwards each time

explanation.surface: A singer's opera features in two return performances, crediting the maestro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two' and 'comebacks' both act on the little word 'in': it is read backwards and then doubled. Arturo Toscanini was the great Italian conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: Arturo Toscanini was the Italian maestro who led La Scala and the NBC Symphony Orchestra.

clue.text: ET has a right to possession

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to keep someone's property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: The extraterrestrial has a claim on property.
explanation.walkthrough: ET, Spielberg's extraterrestrial, is a being from another world.
explanation.definitionFit: Spielberg's ET is an extraterrestrial, a creature from another planet.

clue.text: A big hit for poet

definitions.meaning: in baseball a home run is called by this nickname
the Greek epic poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey

explanation.surface: A great success for a writer of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A home run in baseball has this nickname, and the blind bard of Greek epic bears the same name.

clue.text: Western state with French wine for reformer

parts.note: Cal is an abbreviation for California, a western US state
vin is French for wine

explanation.surface: A Californian goes with French wine for a churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: John Calvin was the Protestant reformer of Geneva.
explanation.definitionFit: John Calvin led the Protestant Reformation in Geneva.

clue.text: I am in the mews, discovering abstract art constructions

indicators.note: the letter is placed inside the building, as 'in' signals

parts.note: a mews was originally a row of stables

explanation.surface: Someone living in a converted mews uncovers modern sculptures.
explanation.walkthrough: Stabiles are Alexander Calder's static abstract sculptures, the stationary counterpart of his mobiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Calder coined the term for his fixed abstract sculptures, as distinct from moving mobiles.

clue.text: One who hid pots and pots of reading matter

definitions.text: One who hid pots and pots of reading matter

parts.words: One who hid pots and pots of reading matter
parts.note: the Dead Sea Scrolls, attributed to a Jewish sect, were hidden in clay jars in the caves of Qumran

explanation.surface: Someone stashed away a large amount of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pots and pots' looks like 'lots', but the scrolls really were hidden in pots; members of this ascetic sect are credited with them.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the ascetic Jewish sect at Qumran, credited with hiding the Dead Sea Scrolls in jars.

clue.text: Fewer methods for identifying one of "these twain"

parts.note: less means fewer in number
ways are methods

explanation.surface: Fewer approaches are needed for recognising one of a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: In Arnold Bennett's trilogy, These Twain are Edwin Clayhanger and Hilda, whose surname titles the second novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilda, heroine of Bennett's Clayhanger trilogy, is half the married couple of These Twain.
